window.near: In a launch window: close to the {{ideal}} km²/s² of the ideal (Hohmann) transfer between these two orbits.
window.far: Far from a launch window: the ideal (Hohmann) transfer between these orbits needs about {{ideal}} km²/s². Windows come round about every {{months}} months, when Earth and Mars line up.

assumptions.Moon: Timing modelled on Apollo 11: about {{coast}} days' coast after leaving Earth orbit, then about {{orbit}} day in lunar orbit before landing. The path is a two-body orbit around the Earth (Lambert's problem) from a parking orbit to where the ephemeris puts the Moon; the Moon's own pull and course corrections are left out. The lunar-orbit loops are drawn, not computed.
assumptions.Mars: The launch date is the one that needs the least launch energy for this landing date, searching {{min}} to {{max}} days of flight. The path is a two-body orbit around the Sun (Lambert's problem) between where the ephemeris puts Earth at launch and Mars at landing; the planets' own pulls near departure and arrival are left out.

sources.title: Sources and methods
sources.intro: Every number in SiteLine is worked out from published data by code in this project; none is typed in by hand. This page brings together how each check works, how we tested it, and every dataset with its licence and link.

methods.positions: Where the Sun and the Earth are, seen from the Moon: NASA JPL's DE440 ephemeris, read with NAIF's SPICE toolkit by our pipeline into a table the app interpolates.
methods.horizon: What the ground hides: from each spot, the horizon is traced in every direction across NASA's LRO LOLA south-pole terrain.
methods.sun: Sunlight: through the {{days}}-day stay we step through time and measure how much of the Sun's disc clears that horizon. The site fails if less than {{pct}}% of the disc is up at any moment, and the moment it drops is found to the minute.
methods.earth: Earth in view, for talking to the lander: the same test for the Earth, counting {{rule}}.
methods.slope: Slope: a lander needs ground flatter than {{deg}}° over 100 m. The loaded terrain is too coarse to see 100 m, so the report says it needs finer terrain instead of guessing.
methods.zone: Artemis zone: the spot must lie south of {{lat}}° latitude.
methods.longTerm: Long-term sunlight and Earth view: maps over a 19-year cycle, computed from the same terrain by the Landfall concept demo, to be replaced by NASA's own product.
methods.planets: The Worlds list and signal delays: distances from the DE440 planet table. A signal's time is that distance divided by the speed of light.
methods.facts: World facts: NASA's planetary fact sheets and NAIF's gravitational parameters. Gravity and escape speed are worked out from them.

earthRule.margin2deg: its centre at least 2° above the horizon

sources.more: The same list is CREDITS.md in the project, and each panel names its own sources too.

panel.heading: Mars
panel.empty: Click anywhere on the planet, or search for a feature, to see what is there.
panel.sources: Heights: NASA MGS MOLA (<megdr>MEGDR</megdr>, made by the MOLA Science Team and archived by the PDS Geosciences Node at Washington University in St. Louis) through <jaanga>Jaanga’s height-map tiles</jaanga>, © 2015 Jaanga authors, <ccby>CC BY 4.0</ccby>, resampled to a coarser grid (about 21 km), so peaks and floors can read a few hundred metres off. Slope shading is computed from these heights, so it has no finer detail than they do. Colour: <sss>Solar System Scope</sss> Mars map, <ccby>CC BY 4.0</ccby>, based on NASA elevation and imagery data and recompressed; the site notes that unmapped gaps in its maps are filled with fictional terrain. Names and feature types: <gaz>IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature</gaz> (USGS), public domain. Details in CREDITS.md.
